I want to be clear that this is not a partisan issue, nor should it ever be treated as one. The suffering of the Syrian people transcends the divisions that too often define our politics in this place.

We have watched, for over a decade now, as a brutal regime has used every tool at its disposal against its own citizens: barrel bombs, chemical weapons, starvation sieges. The international community's response has been, at best, inconsistent, and at worst, an abdication of the very principles we claim to hold dear. I do not say that to score points against any particular Government, because successive Governments of different colours have struggled to find an adequate response to a crisis of this scale.

What I would ask of the Minister today is a clear statement on what more this country intends to do, both in terms of humanitarian assistance and in terms of holding the perpetrators of these atrocities to account. We have heard warm words about accountability mechanisms, about the International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism gathering evidence for future prosecutions, but evidence gathering without prosecution is a promise deferred, not a promise kept.

I would also ask that we not forget the millions of Syrian refugees still living in precarious conditions across the region, in Lebanon, in Jordan, in Turkey, whose hosting nations are themselves buckling under the strain. Our aid budget cuts in recent years have made a real difference to those people, and not for the better.

The people of Syria deserve more than our sympathy. They deserve our sustained, practical commitment, and I will continue to press this Government until they receive it.

My own constituents have seen services cut even as Ministers have stood at that Dispatch Box announcing new investment, and the disconnect between the announcements and the reality on the ground does nothing for public trust in this process.

I would also urge the combined authority, as it finalises its local transport plan, to engage meaningfully with disabled passengers and with community transport providers, who often reach people that mainstream bus services simply do not serve. Low carbon solutions must not mean solutions designed only for those who are already well served by existing infrastructure.

I have spoken with survivors myself, and I can tell the House that what strikes you most is not simply the horror of what they endured, but the quiet dignity with which they carry it, decade after decade, often reliving it in classrooms and community halls because they understand that their testimony is the strongest weapon we have against forgetting.

When the last survivor passes, and that day is coming sooner than any of us would like to admit, we will be left with archives, with photographs, with the testimony that has been so carefully recorded by organisations dedicated to preserving it. But an archive cannot look a room of teenagers in the eye and answer their questions. An archive cannot convey, in the way a living witness can, the sheer human scale of what was lost.

That is precisely why this legislation matters now, while we still have the chance to act with survivors themselves able to see it pass. We owe it to them, and we owe it to the six million who did not survive to tell their own stories, to ensure that denial and distortion are not permitted to fill the space that their absence will leave.

I want to be clear that this is not about restricting legitimate historical inquiry or academic debate. It is about drawing a firm line against the deliberate, malicious distortion of a documented genocide, the kind of distortion we increasingly see spreading unchecked on social media platforms, dressed up as "just asking questions" while it seeds doubt in young and impressionable minds.

I urge all Members to support this Bill, not as a gesture, but as a genuine commitment to the survivors who have trusted us to carry this forward once they no longer can.

The Duke of Edinburgh's Award scheme alone has touched the lives of millions of young people across the Commonwealth, giving them the chance to develop resilience, self-reliance and a sense of achievement that many of them would never otherwise have had the opportunity to discover. We should also remember the personal sacrifice that underpinned his public role: a man who set aside his own naval career, one in which he had shown real distinction, in order to support the Queen in her duties. On behalf of my constituents, I extend our deepest condolences to Her Majesty and the entire Royal Family at this profoundly difficult time.

My son eventually found the courage to speak, and when he did, the room went quiet in a way it had not for any of the other contributions. That tells us something important: young Indigenous voices, when given genuine space rather than a token seat at the table, have the power to reframe an entire conversation. The question is whether we, as legislators, are prepared to build that space as a matter of course, rather than as an exception.

I would ask the Minister what concrete steps are being taken to ensure Indigenous youth are not simply consulted after decisions have effectively been made, but are involved from the earliest stages of policy design. My son deserved better than to sit in that room as an afterthought, and so does every young person like him across this country.

We have talked about ratification for far too long as though it were the finish line, when in truth it is only the starting point. I would particularly highlight the optional protocol, which this motion does not yet commit us to ratifying. Without it, individuals who feel their rights under the convention have been violated have no direct means of bringing a complaint to the UN committee responsible for oversight. That is a significant gap, and I would ask the Minister to explain why we are not moving to ratify the protocol alongside the convention itself, rather than leaving that step for some unspecified future date.

Disabled people and their representative organisations have led this campaign for years, often against considerable institutional inertia, and they deserve to see the fruits of that advocacy translated into real change, not simply a ceremonial signature that changes little in their daily lives.

I commend this motion to the House, while insisting that ratification must be the beginning of a much larger commitment.

This is not an abstract environmental concern for the people I represent. Pacific salmon are woven into the cultural, spiritual and economic fabric of coastal life. For Indigenous nations who have relied on salmon runs for millennia, the collapse of these stocks represents nothing less than a crisis of survival, an erosion of ceremony, of food security, and of a relationship with the land and water that predates this country by thousands of years.

The science is unambiguous. Open-net pen salmon farming has been linked repeatedly to sea lice infestations and disease transmission that devastate wild juvenile salmon as they migrate past farm sites on their way to open ocean. Petitioners are not asking for anything radical; they are asking the Government to follow through on commitments it has already made to transition away from open-net pen farming, commitments that have been repeatedly delayed and diluted under pressure from industry.

I would ask the Minister when we can expect a firm, enforceable timeline for that transition, one that does not leave coastal communities and wild salmon stocks hostage to yet another round of consultations that seem designed to run out the clock rather than deliver real change.

The petitioners who brought this issue to me deserve a real answer, and so do the salmon runs that have sustained this coast since long before any of us were elected to this place.

I want to be honest with the House about the constraints we are operating under. Every cent reduced in excise is a cent less available for public services, for the health budget, for the housing programmes that so many Deputies rightly press me on in this Chamber week after week. We cannot simply keep cutting fuel taxes indefinitely without consequence, however politically tempting that might be in the short term.

That said, I recognise that for people in rural areas without access to reliable public transport, for small businesses reliant on delivery vehicles, and for the haulage sector in particular, fuel costs are not a discretionary expense but a fundamental cost of doing business or simply getting to work. That is precisely why we introduced the diesel rebate scheme, targeted specifically at the haulage sector, to provide relief where it is most needed without applying a blanket reduction that would disproportionately benefit those who can most easily absorb higher costs.

I am keeping the situation under continuous review, and I want to assure Deputy Murphy and others that if the current volatility in international energy markets persists, further measures will be considered. But I would ask Deputies to recognise the genuinely difficult balancing act involved here: protecting households and businesses from the worst of these price shocks, while maintaining the fiscal sustainability that allows us to continue funding essential public services.

I will continue to engage with hauliers' representative groups directly on this matter in the weeks ahead.

We are told, time and again, that action on tax avoidance is a priority, yet when concrete proposals are brought before this House, they are met with the usual excuses: it is too complex, it requires international coordination, it would put Scotland or the UK at a competitive disadvantage. I have heard every one of these excuses rehearsed so many times that I could deliver the Minister's response for him.

The reality is that closing loopholes exploited by multinational corporations and wealthy individuals is not a technical impossibility; it is a question of political priority. Other jurisdictions, some considerably smaller than Scotland, have managed to introduce meaningful transparency measures around beneficial ownership and have taken firmer action against enablers of tax evasion, without the sky falling in on their economies.

I would ask the Minister directly: what estimate has the Treasury made of the revenue lost to the public purse each year through the kind of avoidance schemes this measure claims to address, and does he accept that even partial progress on closing these loopholes would represent a meaningful contribution to public finances at a time when working people across these islands are being asked to shoulder an ever-increasing tax burden themselves?

It cannot be right that ordinary taxpayers, through PAYE, face rigorous and immediate enforcement, while sophisticated avoidance structures used by the wealthiest in our society persist for years, sometimes decades, before any meaningful challenge is mounted. That asymmetry undermines public confidence in the fairness of our tax system as a whole, and it is long past time this Government treated it with the urgency it deserves.

I raise Cardiff's example not simply to praise good local leadership, although that praise is entirely deserved, but to make a wider point about the relationship between local and national government. Time and again during the pandemic, it was local authorities, working closely with community and voluntary organisations, that stepped into the gaps left by a UK Government response that was too often slow, too often centralised, and too often disconnected from the realities faced by communities on the ground.

Cardiff's advice line did not wait for Whitehall guidance before it started fielding calls from anxious families who did not know where their next meal was coming from. Local food banks and mutual aid groups, many staffed entirely by volunteers, filled gaps that no Government department managed to fill in time. That should tell us something important about where the real expertise and responsiveness in our public services actually lies.

As we look ahead to the recovery, I would urge the Government to properly resource local authorities to continue this vital work, rather than expecting councils to deliver on Westminster's ambitions with ever-shrinking budgets. Cardiff and councils like it across Wales have shown what is possible with committed local leadership. Now it is time for national Government to match that commitment with the funding these communities need.

It felt like a rite of passage, walking through those doors with my mother, filling out the little paper form by hand, and watching the clerk stamp my new passbook with what seemed to me, at the time, an almost ceremonial gravity.

I mention this not out of mere nostalgia, although I confess there is plenty of that involved, but because I think we have lost something important in the rush toward an entirely digital banking system. That passbook was more than a record of transactions; it was a tangible, physical relationship with an institution, one that many older people in particular still value and, frankly, still rely on.

I hear regularly from constituents, many of them elderly, some of them living with conditions that make navigating apps and online portals genuinely difficult, who feel increasingly excluded from a banking system that has been redesigned entirely around the assumption that everyone is comfortable managing their finances on a smartphone. For them, the closure of local bank branches is not a minor inconvenience; it is the severing of one of the last remaining points of human contact they have with essential financial services.

I do not say this to argue against digital innovation, which has brought genuine convenience and efficiency to banking for the vast majority of customers. But convenience for the majority cannot come at the cost of exclusion for a significant and vulnerable minority. We need to ensure that alternatives, whether through post offices, community banking hubs, or maintained access to cash, remain genuinely available, not simply promised in a press release while branches continue to close at the current alarming rate.

My mother is no longer with us, but I still think of her whenever I walk past that old branch, now converted into a coffee shop, and I wonder what she would make of the world our banking system has become.

Let me be very clear about what is at stake here. The aluminum and steel sectors in this country support tens of thousands of good, well-paying jobs, many of them in communities where alternative employment opportunities are limited. When we negotiated these thresholds, we did so with the explicit goal of ensuring that vehicles benefiting from preferential trade access under this agreement genuinely reflect North American content, rather than simply being assembled here using components sourced from elsewhere in the world.

The Opposition would have Canadians believe that raising concerns about implementation details is somehow equivalent to abandoning the entire agreement, but that is simply not an honest characterization of the debate we are having today. We can support a good agreement while also insisting on rigorous, transparent enforcement of its provisions. Indeed, that insistence is precisely what protects the gains we have made.

I would remind the House that these thresholds did not appear by accident. They were the product of intense, sustained negotiation with our American and Mexican counterparts, negotiation that required this Government to hold firm against considerable pressure to accept weaker provisions. To suggest now that we should simply wave away concerns about their implementation would be to undermine the very work that secured these protections in the first place.

I will continue to work with industry stakeholders, with labour representatives, and with provincial governments to ensure these provisions are enforced as rigorously as they were negotiated, because Canadian workers deserve nothing less than the full benefit of what this agreement promised them.

This is a structural shock that no reasonable contingency planning could have anticipated. The residents who signed this petition are not asking for special treatment; they are asking for fair treatment, recognition that the pandemic has hit different parts of the country in profoundly different ways, and that a one-size-fits-all funding formula simply cannot capture that reality.

Without additional support, Luton faces the prospect of further cuts to services that families in my constituency, and in that of my hon. I say this not as a complaint about procedure for its own sake, but because the way we schedule our business sends a signal about what we consider important. The matter before us today affects real people, in real and often difficult circumstances, and it deserves better than to be treated as a formality. I would ask the Ceann Comhairle and the Business Committee to give serious consideration to how statements of this nature are scheduled going forward, so that they receive the time and attention commensurate with their importance, rather than being squeezed into whatever slot happens to remain once the more politically prominent business of the day has concluded.

I would also make the point that maximum participation, which this format is nominally designed to allow, is undermined precisely when it is scheduled at times when many Deputies have already left the Chamber for constituency commitments or other obligations. There is a real tension between the theory of these statements and the practice of how they are actually delivered.

I hope that going forward, we can find a better balance, one that respects both the practical demands on Deputies' time and the genuine importance of the issues we are here to discuss.

These are children who are already in the care of the State, children whom we as legislators have a direct and unambiguous responsibility to protect, and yet they remain disproportionately vulnerable to exploitation by predators who deliberately target the most vulnerable young people in our society.

I want to ask the Minister what specific steps have been taken since 2019 to address the particular vulnerabilities of children in care to sexual exploitation. Have staffing levels in social work teams been increased to allow for the kind of close, consistent relationships that research consistently shows are protective against exploitation? Has training been rolled out across residential and foster care settings to help carers recognise the early warning signs?

We know from Barnardo's own casework, and from similar research conducted internationally, that children who have experienced instability in their care placements, who have been moved multiple times between different settings, are at significantly higher risk. That instability is often driven not by any failure of individual social workers, who are frequently working under impossible caseloads, but by a systemic shortage of appropriate placements across the country.

I would also highlight the particular risks associated with unregulated and semi-independent living arrangements for older children in care, settings that have expanded in recent years precisely because of the shortage of appropriate residential placements, but which often lack the level of supervision needed to protect vulnerable teenagers from those who would seek to exploit them.

These 498 children are not a statistic to be filed away. Each one represents a failure of protection that this House has a duty to address with urgency, not with another report that gathers dust on a shelf.

We are talking about people on fixed incomes who have already made every possible economy in their household budgets, who cannot simply absorb another significant increase in their heating and lighting bills without making impossible choices between eating and staying warm.

I have lost count of the number of constituents who have written to me describing exactly this dilemma. One pensioner in my constituency told me she had started spending her afternoons in the local library, not to read, but simply to stay warm without running her own heating. That is the reality facing older people across this country, and it is a direct consequence of decisions made in this House.

The scrapping of free TV licences for the over-75s was a betrayal of a promise made repeatedly by this Government, and it has left hundreds of thousands of pensioners, many of them isolated and living alone, having to find an additional £159 a year at precisely the moment they can least afford it. That decision, combined with the failure to properly uprate pensions in line with the real cost of living pensioners actually face, has left our older generation dangerously exposed.

I would ask the Minister what specific, targeted support will be made available before winter sets in, not vague commitments to review the situation, but concrete measures that pensioners can rely on now. The triple lock, whatever its imperfections, exists precisely to protect pensioners from exactly this kind of cost of living shock, and any suggestion of watering it down further would be an unconscionable betrayal at the worst possible moment.

Too often in this House, we debate spending decisions purely in terms of their immediate cost and immediate benefit, as though the consequences of our choices simply evaporate the moment a budget year closes. But that is not how infrastructure works, it is not how debt works, and it is certainly not how our natural environment works. A road built today shapes commuting patterns for decades. A pension liability incurred today falls on taxpayers who have not yet been born. A wetland drained today cannot simply be recreated when a future generation realises its value.

I would like to see this House adopt something closer to a formal intergenerational impact assessment for major spending and infrastructure decisions, similar to models that have been trialled in Wales through their Well-being of Future Generations Act. That legislation requires public bodies to consider the long-term impact of their decisions, and while its implementation has not been without challenges, it represents exactly the kind of institutional discipline that could help correct the short-termism that so often characterises political decision-making in systems built around electoral cycles of four or five years.

The temptation in any democracy is to prioritise the visible, immediate benefit over the diffuse, long-term cost, because the electoral rewards for the former are so much clearer than for the latter. But that temptation is precisely why we need structural mechanisms, built into how this House scrutinises spending, to force genuine consideration of intergenerational fairness into decisions that will outlast any of us currently sitting in this Chamber.

I raise it because there is a pattern, I think, in how this House sometimes conducts itself: grand declarations about the importance of an issue, delivered with great rhetorical flourish, followed by a rather more modest commitment of actual time and attention once the cameras and the immediate opportunity for a soundbite have passed.

If Members genuinely believe a debate to be of the significance they claim in their speeches, I would gently suggest that significance ought to be reflected in their willingness to remain present for its duration, to hear the contributions of colleagues who take a different view, and to engage with the substance of the arguments being made rather than simply delivering a prepared statement and departing.

This is not, I hasten to add, a criticism confined to any single party or any single Member. It is a broader observation about parliamentary practice that I think deserves reflection from all sides of this House. Debate, properly understood, is a genuinely deliberative exercise, not merely a sequence of individual statements delivered to an increasingly empty Chamber.

I thank you for allowing me to raise this point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker, and I hope it might prompt some reflection, even if I do not expect it to change longstanding habits overnight.

Freedom of religion or belief is a fundamental human right, enshrined in international law, yet it remains one of the most systematically violated rights across the globe, affecting communities of every faith, and indeed those of no faith at all, who continue to face persecution, discrimination and, in the most severe cases, genocide, simply because of what they believe or do not believe.

I want to highlight, in the time I have available, the particular situation facing religious minorities in a number of countries where this Government has significant diplomatic and trade relationships, relationships that I believe give us real leverage to press for improved protections, if only we were prepared to use that leverage with genuine consistency, rather than allowing commercial considerations to routinely take precedence over human rights concerns when the two come into tension.

We have seen, time and again, this Government express genuine and sincere-sounding concern about specific cases of religious persecution, only for that concern to feature rather less prominently in the actual conduct of our trade negotiations and diplomatic relationships with the countries responsible. I do not say this to suggest bad faith on the part of Ministers, many of whom I know to be genuinely committed to this cause, but to highlight a structural tension within Government policy that needs to be resolved rather than perpetually managed.

I would ask the Minister what specific mechanisms exist to ensure that freedom of religion or belief considerations are genuinely embedded within our trade policy decisions, not simply raised as a secondary concern once commercial agreements have already been substantially negotiated.

We need a genuine industrial strategy that diversifies our economy away from this boom-and-bust dependency on commodity price cycles, investing seriously in value-added manufacturing, in renewable energy infrastructure, and in the skills training needed to help workers transition into these more stable and sustainable sectors of employment.

I would ask the Minister what plan exists to claw back the corporate bailout funds that were distributed to companies like Loblaws without adequate conditions attached, conditions that should have prevented exactly the kind of layoffs and hazard pay cuts we subsequently witnessed. I have listened carefully to those who argue that alternative arrangements, whatever precise form they might take, could deliver the same outcome without the backstop's specific mechanism. I remain to be convinced, because every serious, independent technical assessment I have seen of these alternative proposals has identified significant unresolved questions about how they would actually function in practice, particularly given the unique political and historical sensitivities that make any visible infrastructure on this particular border so uniquely fraught.

The Taoiseach has been consistent and, in my view, entirely correct in insisting that any withdrawal agreement must include a legally binding guarantee against a hardening of the border, not simply a political commitment that could be abandoned or reinterpreted once the wider negotiations move on to the future relationship phase.

I would urge those in this House and in the other jurisdiction who continue to search for alternatives to recognise that the backstop was never designed as an ideological preference, but as the practical, workable solution to a problem that any credible alternative must solve just as effectively, not merely gesture toward solving through aspiration alone.

It is a zero-sum framing of human dignity that has no basis in lived reality, but it persists precisely because it is emotionally effective, tapping into genuine anxieties about change and translating them into hostility toward the group being discussed, rather than toward whatever underlying economic or social pressures are actually driving those anxieties.

We have seen this exact pattern repeat itself across history, applied to different groups at different times, always with the same underlying structure: a vulnerable or marginalised community is identified, their pursuit of basic dignity and equal treatment is reframed as an aggressive imposition upon the majority, and fear is mobilised to resist a change that, once achieved, is almost always found to have cost the majority nothing at all.

I think it falls to all of us in this House, regardless of our party affiliation, to name this pattern clearly whenever we encounter it, rather than allowing it to pass unchallenged simply because confronting it directly can feel politically uncomfortable or risks being characterised as partisan point-scoring. Silence in the face of this argument does not represent neutrality; it represents, in practice, a form of tacit permission for it to continue shaping public discourse unchecked.

I would encourage every Member of this House to consider how this same rhetorical pattern might be showing up in debates we are currently having, not simply in the historical examples that are easier for us to recognise with the benefit of hindsight, but in the live political arguments unfolding around us today, where the same insidious logic often hides behind more contemporary and superficially reasonable-sounding language.

We owe it to those our decisions affect to see this pattern for what it is, and to name it honestly.
